slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: How machines built like us are entering our homes, factories, and daily lives

slides.heading: Why Human-Shaped Robots?
slides.body: Our world is designed for human bodies — doors, stairs, tools, vehicles. A robot with two arms and two legs can operate in the same spaces and use the same equipment as a person, without redesigning the environment around it.

slides.heading: The Key Players Racing Ahead
slides.body: Figure AI, Tesla Optimus, Boston Dynamics Atlas, and Agility Robotics' Digit are leading the charge. Backed by billions in investment, each is targeting industrial labor first before moving into consumer and healthcare markets.

slides.heading: AI Is the Missing Ingredient
slides.body: Earlier humanoid robots were brittle — they followed rigid scripts. Today's models use foundation AI models trained on video and sensor data, letting them adapt to novel situations, recover from slips, and learn new tasks from human demonstrations.

slides.heading: What They Can Already Do
slides.body: Current humanoid robots can sort packages, fold laundry, carry boxes up stairs, open doors, and assist on factory assembly lines. Some can now work full shifts at real facilities without human intervention.

slides.heading: The Labor Shortage Driver
slides.body: An aging global population is creating acute shortages in elder care, logistics, and manufacturing. Humanoid robots are seen not just as efficiency tools, but as a necessary workforce supplement to keep economies running.

slides.heading: The Hard Engineering Problems
slides.body: Battery life remains the biggest constraint — most robots run 2–4 hours on a charge. Dexterous hand manipulation, walking on uneven terrain, and real-time decision-making under uncertainty are still active research frontiers.

slides.heading: Safety and Ethics Questions
slides.body: As robots work alongside humans, questions arise: Who is liable when a robot causes harm? How do we prevent misuse as surveillance tools? Labor advocates warn of job displacement without adequate social safety nets to absorb the impact.

slides.heading: The Cost Curve Is Falling Fast
slides.body: Early humanoid prototypes cost $500,000+. Mass production targets now aim for units under $30,000 by the late 2020s — comparable to a mid-range car. Falling sensor and actuator costs are making this trajectory realistic.

slides.heading: The Robot Decade Has Begun
slides.body: Humanoid robots will not arrive all at once — but they are arriving. The decisions we make now about deployment, safety, and labor policy will shape whether this technology uplifts humanity or deepens inequality.
